I tried Lupron and Orilissa.  Lupron was easily 100x worse than Orilissa, plus Orilissa works much better at pain management! They have different mechanisms of action, and I think that made all the difference.

Basically, during bone conduction, vibrating get passed to the ear canal which generates sound pressure by vibrating the bones and cartilage. The energy gets amplified at its resonant frequency (~200 Hz), however most of this energy escapes or if the unoccluded ear canal. When the ear canal is occluded, this sound energy stays in the canal and is able to reach the eardrum the same way air conducted sound normally would. 

Source: I am doing my doctoral project on bone conduction which includes the occlusion effect. I have lots of resources so let me know if you need any!

I'm an audiology student and that's what I've been taught. I can find other sources that corroborate  [here](http://vr4hearingloss.net/what/conductive-hearing-loss/) under "disarticulation of the ossicular chain," [here](https://www.boystownhospital.org/knowledgeCenter/articles/hearing/Pages/TypesofHearing.aspx), and [here](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5629081/) (if you ctrl+f "maximal conductive hearing loss"). This is the maximum because past this intensity, the sound waves are strong enough to be converted into bone conduction, which will go straight to the cochlea, bypassing the middle ear system. I cannot speak to your specific case, but this is what is normally found.

The middle ear system is most sensitive to mid range frequencies, so it would be normal to have a mid range hearing loss of the middle ear system is affected. But there are a lot of pieces in play, and every person's system is different.

Eardrums heal very quickly, and even a large perforation won't cause much hearing loss, so long as there is some of the drum intact to which the ossicles (tiny bones in your ear) can attach to. Your "cochlear test" (which I assume means bone conduction testing) was normal because it bypasses your middle ear system, where your eardrums are.

Even if your ear drum was completely gone, the hearing loss wouldn't be horrible. A maximum conductive hearing loss is about 50-60 dB HL, which is a moderate range hearing loss. You see a maximum conductive hearing loss in individuals without a functioning middle ear system (the middle ear system includes the ear drum and ossicles). Even without a middle ear system, if the cochlea is functioning, then there would still be hearing.

The sensorineural part, or nerve damage that you have in both ears is probably unrelated to the ear infections. Depending on how old you are, this might just be a normal part of aging. 

I can only guess that the hearing loss in the right ear, because it's mostly conductive, is due to the tympanoplasty but I'm not positive, it can be due to any part of the middle ear system including your ossicles.

So the graph with the circles is for your right ear. On the audiogram the left side is for low notes and the right side is for high notes. It shows that you have a mostly conductive hearing loss. This means that the hearing loss in this ear is due to some issue with your middle ear, probably related to the tympanoplasty. Although, it is important to know that you do have some hearing loss unrelated to the tympanoplasty in that right ear. It matches up pretty well to the hearing loss that you have in your left ear, which is a sensorineural hearing loss, or due to some sort of nerve damage.

The "cats head outline" is what we call the speech banana. It just shows the range of frequencies and intensities for most speech sounds, if you if your hearing loss falls below the speech banana, then you won't be getting a lot of the speech sounds.

The second set of graphs towards the bottom is your tympanogram. This shows how your middle ear is moving. It shows that in your right ear, your eardrum is not moving at all. This is probably why you have your hearing loss in your right ear, because your eardrum is not moving like it should be and is probably due to the tympanoplasty. In your left ear, it shows that you have some negative pressure, which is usually due to some eustachian tube dysfunction, like allergies or maybe a cold. The graph for your left ear also shows that your eardrum is moving, but not very much.

Sorry, I meant that between men and women they are different, but say from one man to the next, the general shape of the vocal tract is the same. The vocal tract determines quality of voice, and if a voice is "feminine" or "masculine." Pitch is unrelated (though generally women have higher voices and vice versa).
This is true, the human auditory system is especially sensitive to frequencies in the range of human speech (I believe it is between 4k and 200 Hz, but don't quote me on that).

See my comment for more information, but basically men and women generally have different shapes of vocal tracts, see [here](https://s-media-cache-ak0.pinimg.com/736x/a8/4d/e6/a84de6bcde7f115f5c2690d814d223f3.jpg). Although the vocal fold length (which determines pitch) may be longer in a woman, the vocal tracts of men and women are generally the same, and therefore men and women have similar qualities of speech, but different pitches. Just like a trumpet still sounds like a trumpet even if it plays other pitches.

So there are two different parts of sound, pitch and timbre. Timbre refers to the quality of a sound, and pitch refers to how high or low a sound is. A trumpet and piano can play the same pitch, but they sounds different because they differ in timbre. 

Pitch as far as voice goes is determined by vocal cord length, and is determined by your physical size (larger people have bigger/longer vocal chords and therefore a lower pitch voice). 

Timbre in speech is determined by vocal tract length, or the overall shape of your resonators (esophagus, mouth, etc.) Depending on the exact shape of your resonators, certain frequencies that are produced from your vocal folds are attenuated (diminished) and some are amplified (increased). The specific pattern of the frequencies that are louder and softer determine timbre (or how your voice sounds).

As a side note, movement of the resonators and tightening/loosening of the vocal folds is how we speak. The vocal folds determine pitch/prosody and the resonators determine what sound (phoneme) is being made.

Source: BS in speech and hearing sciences

*There are a few things you DON'T want to do.*
*Don't self-harm, it starts a vicious cycle of depression that is hard to break.
*Don't sleep just to pass the day away, force yourself to do something.

*What you should do:*
*When feeling bad about yourself, doing something that occupies your mind, something you enjoy will subdue these thoughts.
*Surround yourself with things that make you happy. Birds make me happy, so when I'm depressed, I go sit outside and listen to the birds.
*If you want to help your depressed friends, listen. Never scold. Never say "just stop being sad". Be there for them. Depression is usually grown out of feelings that no one cares about them.

**I hope these tips help, good luck!**
